``` ## About the project Our group of six acted as a consulting firm, A & A Consultancy, tasked with producing a full strategic review of Superdry, the British apparel brand that rose to become a FTSE-listed retailer and then collapsed into retrenchment and delisting. The report examined how the brand captured value in its early years, why it declined through overexpansion and brand dilution, and what strategic interventions could restore its competitive position. The analysis followed a structured consulting process of **Orientation, Diagnostics, Intervention, Evaluation**, applying frameworks including PESTEL, Porter's Five Forces, SWOT, RBV/VRIO, the Strategy Diamond and the ERRC Grid. As Associate Director I led analysis and synthesis work particularly across the Diagnostics and Evaluation stages, with input from the team across every section. The group built the underlying insights; this page rebuilds the key visual artefacts as interactive Plotly and Mermaid renders for the portfolio. ::: {.callout-note title="What's on this page"} The visualisations below reproduce the core strategic artefacts from the Group BS1 Superdry report. Financial data comes from Superdry's publicly reported annual accounts (FY2014 to FY2024); the framework scoring reflects our group's consensus diagnostic rather than external research. The original report used static exhibits; this page rebuilds the same underlying analysis as executable Python with Plotly, plus Mermaid for the conceptual diagrams, as a portfolio extension. ::: ## 1. The decline in numbers Superdry's financial trajectory tells the story more clearly than any framework. Revenue more than doubled between FY2014 and FY2018 as the brand rode its Japanese-Americana aesthetic to global expansion. From the FY2018 peak onward, decline was continuous through a combination of brand dilution, perpetual discounting, structural retail pressure, and the pandemic. By FY2024 revenue had fallen to roughly 56% of its peak, and the company was taken private that July[^superdry]. [^superdry]: Superdry plc, Annual Reports FY2014 to FY2024. Figures approximated from publicly filed accounts for illustrative purposes. FY2024 revenue reflects the last full financial year before delisting from the London Stock Exchange on 1 July 2024. ::: {#cell-fig-revenue-history .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import plotly.graph_objects as go revenue_history = pd.DataFrame({ "Year": ["FY14", "FY15", "FY16", "FY17", "FY18", "FY19", "FY20", "FY21", "FY22", "FY23", "FY24"], "Revenue": [430, 486, 590, 752, 872, 872, 705, 556, 610, 622, 488], "Phase": ["Growth", "Growth", "Growth", "Growth", "Peak", "Peak", "Decline", "Decline", "Stabilisation", "Stabilisation", "Retrenchment"], }) phase_colours = { "Growth": "#1e7e34", "Peak": "#d4a017", "Decline": "#c8102e", "Stabilisation": "#4a90a4", "Retrenchment": "#6c757d", } fig = go.Figure() fig.add_trace(go.Scatter( x=revenue_history["Year"], y=revenue_history["Revenue"], mode="lines+markers", line=dict(color="#1a1a1a", width=2.5), marker=dict( size=11, color=[phase_colours[p] for p in revenue_history["Phase"]], line=dict(color="white", width=1.5), ), text=[f"£{v}m" for v in revenue_history["Revenue"]], hovertemplate="%{x}
Revenue: %{text}

July 2024", showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, arrowcolor="#6c757d", ax=-30, ay=-50, font=dict(size=11, color="#1a1a1a")) for phase, colour in phase_colours.items(): fig.add_trace(go.Scatter( x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=10, color=colour), name=phase, showlegend=True, )) fig.update_layout( height=460, margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=30, b=30), paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"), xaxis=dict(showgrid=False), yaxis=dict(title="Revenue (£ millions)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#eee", range=[350, 950]), legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, x=0), ) fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-revenue-history .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Superdry annual revenue, FY2014 to FY2024. The brand doubled revenue in four years to an FY2018 peak of roughly £872m, then lost the majority of that growth over the following six years. The company was taken private in July 2024. ::: ::: The five phases shown above map directly onto the strategic narrative of the report: an early Growth period built on differentiated brand identity, a Peak where over-expansion and licensing began diluting the equity, a Decline accelerated by pandemic demand shifts and the cost-of-living crisis, a Stabilisation as the founder returned and discounting was reduced, and the current Retrenchment back to core markets. ## 2. Industry attractiveness: Porter's Five Forces Applying Porter's Five Forces to the apparel sector shows why Superdry's current mid-market position is structurally exposed. Four of the five forces register at High or Medium-High intensity. The scoring below is our group's consensus assessment from the Diagnostics stage, with supporting logic in the report. ::: {#cell-fig-five-forces .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import plotly.graph_objects as go forces = pd.DataFrame({ "Force": [ "Competitive rivalry", "Buyer power", "Threat of substitutes", "Threat of new entrants", "Supplier power", ], "Score": [5, 5, 5, 4, 3], "Evidence": [ "Fast fashion (Shein, Boohoo), sportswear giants (Nike, Adidas), heritage revival (Barbour)", "Low switching costs, price transparency, loyalty shift from brand to value", "Athleisure, second-hand markets, rental services", "E-commerce lowers barriers but brand equity still hard to build", "Moderate concentration in global apparel supply chains", ], }) fig = go.Figure() fig.add_trace(go.Scatterpolar( r=list(forces["Score"]) + [forces["Score"].iloc[0]], theta=list(forces["Force"]) + [forces["Force"].iloc[0]], fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(200,16,46,0.20)", line=dict(color="#c8102e", width=2.5), marker=dict(size=10, color="#c8102e"), text=forces["Evidence"].tolist() + [forces["Evidence"].iloc[0]], hovertemplate="%{theta}
Intensity: %{r}/5
%{text}", name="Force intensity", )) fig.update_layout( polar=dict( radialaxis=dict(visible=True, range=[0, 5], tickvals=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], ticktext=["1", "2", "3", "4", "5"], gridcolor="#ddd", linecolor="#ddd"), angularaxis=dict(gridcolor="#ddd", linecolor="#ddd"), bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", ), height=480, margin=dict(l=60, r=60, t=30, b=30), paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"), showlegend=False, ) fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-five-forces .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Porter's Five Forces acting on Superdry. Scores from 1 (low intensity) to 5 (high intensity) reflect the Group BS1 diagnostic assessment. Four of the five forces sit at high or medium-high intensity, giving an overall low industry attractiveness for an undifferentiated mid-market player. ::: ::: The implication is blunt: Superdry cannot win by trying to out-compete Shein on price or Nike on scale. A mid-market undifferentiated player in this industry structure has no natural profit pool. Either re-establish meaningful differentiation or continue margin compression indefinitely. ## 3. The Value Stick, shortened The Value Stick concept frames strategic value capture as the vertical distance between a customer's willingness to pay (WTP) at the top and the firm's cost at the bottom, with price sitting in between. A healthy brand runs a long stick: high WTP, controlled costs, room for both consumer surplus and firm margin. Superdry's decline can be read cleanly on this frame. Between 2012 and 2023, WTP compressed (the brand lost its premium cachet), costs rose (through discounting, logistics complexity and wholesale dilution), and the stick shortened dramatically. ::: {#cell-fig-value-stick .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import plotly.graph_objects as go from plotly.subplots import make_subplots fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("2012: Peak Superdry", "2023: Diluted brand"), horizontal_spacing=0.2) peak_wtp, peak_price, peak_cost = 100, 70, 35 fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Peak"], y=[peak_cost], name="Cost", marker=dict(color="#6c757d"), showlegend=True, text=f"£{peak_cost}", textposition="inside", textfont=dict(color="white", size=14)), row=1, col=1) fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Peak"], y=[peak_price - peak_cost], name="Firm margin", marker=dict(color="#1e7e34"), showlegend=True, text=f"£{peak_price - peak_cost}", textposition="inside", textfont=dict(color="white", size=14)), row=1, col=1) fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Peak"], y=[peak_wtp - peak_price], name="Consumer surplus", marker=dict(color="#c8e6c9"), showlegend=True, text=f"£{peak_wtp - peak_price}", textposition="inside", textfont=dict(color="#1a1a1a", size=14)), row=1, col=1) dil_wtp, dil_price, dil_cost = 55, 40, 32 fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Diluted"], y=[dil_cost], name="Cost", marker=dict(color="#6c757d"), showlegend=False, text=f"£{dil_cost}", textposition="inside", textfont=dict(color="white", size=14)), row=1, col=2) fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Diluted"], y=[dil_price - dil_cost], name="Firm margin", marker=dict(color="#1e7e34"), showlegend=False, text=f"£{dil_price - dil_cost}", textposition="inside", textfont=dict(color="white", size=14)), row=1, col=2) fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Diluted"], y=[dil_wtp - dil_price], name="Consumer surplus", marker=dict(color="#c8e6c9"), showlegend=False, text=f"£{dil_wtp - dil_price}", textposition="inside", textfont=dict(color="#1a1a1a", size=14)), row=1, col=2) fig.add_annotation(x="Peak", y=peak_wtp, text=f"WTP £{peak_wtp}", showarrow=False, yshift=14, font=dict(size=12, color="#1a1a1a"), row=1, col=1) fig.add_annotation(x="Diluted", y=dil_wtp, text=f"WTP £{dil_wtp}", showarrow=False, yshift=14, font=dict(size=12, color="#1a1a1a"), row=1, col=2) fig.update_layout( barmode="stack", height=480, margin=dict(l=40, r=40, t=50, b=30), paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"), legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.12, x=0.25), ) fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 115], showgrid=True, gridcolor="#eee", title="£") fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False) fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-value-stick .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` The Value Stick concept applied to Superdry. Left: peak 2012 positioning with strong WTP, controlled cost base and visible margin. Right: 2023 after dilution, with compressed WTP, higher effective costs and negligible margin. Figures are illustrative to show the directional shift. ::: ::: The key observation is that margin (green) shrinks sharply even though the firm lowered price. Cost did not fall proportionately because discounting behaviour, wholesale concessions and licensing overheads added hidden complexity. This is the vicious cycle described in the report's Diagnostics section: low-margin, volume-based economic logic that destroys brand value and profitability simultaneously. ## 4. SWOT synthesis The internal analysis surfaced a stark gap between genuine residual strengths (brand recognition, design archive, founder-led creative direction) and acute weaknesses (brand dilution, weak digital, high-cost legacy model, debt overhang). The matrix below summarises the full SWOT from the report. ```{=html}

Strengths

  • Global brand recognition
  • Distinctive design DNA
  • Founder-led creative direction restored
  • Established retail presence

Weaknesses

  • Severe brand dilution from over-licensing
  • Perpetual discounting eroding equity
  • Weak digital and DTC capabilities
  • Wholesale-reliant high-cost model
  • Crippling debt burden

Opportunities

  • Sustainability / circular fashion
  • Digital transformation & DTC
  • Refocus core markets & categories
  • Experiential retail using heritage

Threats

  • Fierce competition (Shein, Nike)
  • Higher sustainability expectations
  • Cost-of-living pressure on premium
  • Heritage strategy risks becoming dated

Figure 4: Superdry SWOT matrix

``` Viewed as a diagnostic rather than an inventory, the SWOT makes two points clear. First, the strengths are heritage assets: real but finite, and they depreciate fast without investment. Second, the weaknesses and threats reinforce each other (perpetual discounting plus cost-of-living pressure plus weak digital plus fierce competition form a trap). Any renewal strategy has to break that reinforcing loop. ## 5. Strategy Diamond: where the trade-offs went wrong Hambrick and Fredrickson's Strategy Diamond frames a strategy as five interlocking elements that must reinforce each other: **Arenas, Vehicles, Differentiators, Staging, and Economic Logic**. The report's Diagnostics section used the Diamond to synthesise Superdry's historical mis-steps into a single integrated picture. ```{=html}

Figure 5: Strategy Diamond applied to Superdry's historical strategy. Each element traded away its original strength, and the elements ceased to reinforce each other.

``` ::: {.callout-tip title="The Economic Logic element is the hinge"} All four other elements can be fixed tactically. The Economic Logic shift from premium value-based to low-margin volume-based is the one that structurally reset the cost base, and unwinding it requires rebuilding willingness to pay first. That sequencing is what the report's Evaluation section addresses through the phased roadmap below. ::: ## 6. Roadmap to renewal The Evaluation stage proposes a three-phase roadmap that sequences the renewal correctly: stabilise before investing, invest before embedding. Each phase has distinct owners, metrics and strategic outcomes, aligned with the recommendations developed in the Intervention stage. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-roadmap %%| fig-cap: "Three-phase renewal roadmap. Short-term stabilisation creates the credibility and operational room for medium-term capability investment; long-term embedding of sustainability, digital and purpose transforms the strategy from retrenchment into sustainable differentiation." %%{init: {'securityLevel': 'loose'}}%% flowchart LR A["0-12 MONTHS
Stabilise & Align
• Reset brand purpose
• Reduce discounting
• Restructure teams
• Stabilise operations"] B["12-30 MONTHS
Build & Transform
• Digital-first capabilities
• E-commerce upgrade
• Experiential flagships
• Sustainability lines"] C["30+ MONTHS
Embed & Sustain
• Balanced Scorecard
• Continuous innovation
• Sustainability routines
• Purpose-led leadership"] A --> B --> C style A fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100,color:#1a1a1a,stroke-width:2px style B fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1976d2,color:#1a1a1a,stroke-width:2px style C fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#1e7e34,color:#1a1a1a,stroke-width:2px ``` Each phase is designed to address a specific risk revealed by the Diagnostics. Phase 1 addresses the cash-flow and credibility risk. Phase 2 addresses the capability gap in digital and sustainability that the RBV/VRIO exposed. Phase 3 addresses the strategic drift risk by embedding the new logic in day-to-day performance management, not just strategic statements. ## My role as Associate Director ```{=html}
Diagnostic lead
Led analysis and synthesis work through the Diagnostics stage, coordinating the group's PESTEL and Porter's Five Forces assessments and integrating them with the internal analyses into a single strategic picture.
Framework application
Contributed to the Strategy Diamond synthesis, particularly the Economic Logic element where Superdry's shift from premium to volume-based thinking emerged as the structural hinge of the decline story.
Evaluation logic
Helped shape the Evaluation stage logic that tests each recommendation against the specific diagnostic issue it addresses, ensuring the roadmap was a coherent response to the problem rather than a generic retail playbook.
Presentation contribution
Co-presented the analytical sections of the group's strategy pitch. The team acknowledges the live presentation had coordination issues that we worked through together afterwards to strengthen the final report.
``` ## Reflection This was my first experience working in a consulting format with a formally defined team structure and a real business case. The most valuable lesson was learning how frameworks that look mechanical on the page (PESTEL, Five Forces, Strategy Diamond) function very differently when applied to an actual declining company with incomplete information. The Strategy Diamond in particular was initially treated by the group as a five-box summary exercise and only became useful when we started arguing about which of the five elements was the hinge. That debate (which we eventually resolved on the Economic Logic element) was the point at which our analysis graduated from description into diagnosis. The group dynamics were the other major learning. We hit a rough patch around the in-module presentation, where last-minute slide changes combined with IT issues produced a coordination failure that was uncomfortable at the time. Working through it afterwards, with a combination of honest conversation and shared resolve to make the report itself a strong piece of work, taught me more about managing team pressure than the frameworks themselves did. The skills matrix we drew up early in the project (a consulting tool I had not encountered before) turned out to be the single most useful organisational device we used, because it gave each member a defensible domain and reduced duplication. Reproducing the analytical exhibits as interactive Python and Mermaid renders for this portfolio was a separate exercise from the module itself. The original report used static diagrams embedded in a designed PDF. Rebuilding them forced me to re-examine whether each framework actually added unique insight, or whether some were decorative rather than diagnostic. The Porter's Five Forces radar and the Value Stick are, on reflection, the two frameworks that pulled the most analytical weight in the final argument. The others supported that argument rather than producing it independently. Strategy as a discipline is less about running more frameworks and more about choosing the two or three that matter for the specific question, then applying them rigorously enough to produce a decision. That was the takeaway I carried out of the module, and it is the lens I intend to apply to business analytics roles where the risk is usually the same: too many dashboards, not enough diagnosis. ## Downloads ```{=html}
